items.title: Is library building obsoleted by AI coding?
items.body: Huge open source projects have been successful by building upon dozens to hundreds of small libraries that encapsulate functionality and complexity. AI coding uses these libraries to quickly build applications. With the latest round of model releases I am seeing that AI can now generate the functionality of almost any library in-line as it generates the application. When building took a long time, breaking things down into well defined modules, shipping incrementally, and reusing code, were essential techniques. They seem much less important when AI is doing the work. Is software library creation obsolete?

Customization: Optimizing Compiler Technology for SELF, a Dynamically-Typed Object-Oriented Programming Language (1989)
items.body: Dynamically-typed object-oriented languages please programmers, but their lack of static type information penalizes performance. Our new implementation techniques extract static type information from declaration-free programs. Our system compiles several copies of a given procedure, each customized for one receiver type, so that the type of the receiver is bound at compile time. The compiler predicts types that are statically unknown but likely, and inserts run-time type tests to verify its predictions. It splits calls, compiling a copy on each control path, optimized to the specific types on that path. items.title: Why don’t more developers "use the platform"?
How I Found 12 Testers for Google Play Closed Testing, Twice
items.body:
Friends and family for my first app, Reddit “test for test” for the second, plus a Reddit post template you can copy.
 

 Over the past months, I built and shipped two Android apps on my own. I wanted hands-on experience with Kotlin Multiplatform and with taking an app all the way from an idea to Google Play. The first one is an exam prep app for the German citizenship test. The second one is a grid-based puzzle game that challenges your focus and memory. 

 Writing the code was the part I expected to be hard. The part that surprised me was closed testing. items.title: I built a tiny tool that catches the "printed at 94%" problem
items.body:
Hi everyone, 

 I built  a free print scale checker  as part of my printer test site, after running into a frustrating problem: prints that look fine but come out the wrong size. 

 The usual cause: an A4 file printed on Letter with "Fit to page" on shrinks to about 94%. Nothing looks broken, but templates, labels and patterns are off. 

  What I focused on:  

 
 Print one sheet, measure a 100 mm bar, type the number 
 It tells you the scale and whether it matches a paper-size mismatch 
 Runs in the browser, nothing uploaded 
 

  What I learned:  

 
 "The printer printed" and "it printed correctly" are different checks 
 Real vector PDFs beat HTML print for exact sizes 
 

  Question for developers:  have you built anything that has to print at an exact size? How did you test it?
